topic: Should you follow rules you disagree with?

messages.speaker: kant
messages.content:
The question conflates two things I spent an essay separating. In What is Enlightenment? I distinguished the public use of reason, which must always be free, from the private use, which may rightly be constrained. The officer obeys the order and then, as a scholar addressing the world, argues in print that the order is foolish. Argue as much as you like, about whatever you like, but obey. Without the first, no enlightenment; without the second, no civil condition at all, and the civil condition is the ground on which arguing becomes possible.

But mark the limit, for I am not preaching servility. A rule that would require me to treat humanity, in myself or another, merely as a means, that rule I cannot follow, because I could not will it as law at all. Disagreement is not the threshold. Contradiction with the moral law is.

messages.speaker: taleb
messages.content:
Professor, with respect, your officer is my exhibit A. He follows the order, the campaign fails, and who pays? Not the theorist of orders. The first question about any rule is never whether I agree with it; it is who bears the harm if the rule is wrong. A rule written by people exposed to its consequences, follow it even when you disagree, because it encodes the scar tissue of everyone it already burned. Grandmother's rules are in this class; they have survived contact with centuries. A rule written by a committee insulated from its own errors deserves exactly the deference it gives to reality: none.

Skin in the game is the filter, and it is an old one; I stole it from Hammurabi, whose builder sleeps under the house he built. Your categorical imperative, meanwhile, universalizes beautifully and pays no invoice. I trust the doorman's rulebook over the ethicist's, and I have the P&L to explain why.

messages.speaker: confucius
messages.content:
You both speak of rules as a fence between yourself and others' errors. Permit an older view: the rites are not a fence; they are a grammar. When I entered the great temple, I asked about everything, and someone sneered that the man from Zou knew no ritual. Asking, I said, is the ritual. The form is how reverence becomes visible; followed emptily, it is nothing; a man without humaneness, what has he to do with ritual?

So, should you follow rules you disagree with? Wrong order of questions. First: have you practiced the rule long enough to disagree with it from inside? The student who finds the bow pointless in his first year has discovered nothing about the bow. And when disagreement survives practice, the Way is not defiance but remonstrance: serve your lord, oppose him to his face when he errs, gently, repeatedly, and remain at your post. My disciples recorded me saying that a gentleman in remonstrating may be worn out, but he does not abandon the relationship. The rule and the disagreement travel together, inside loyalty.

messages.speaker: kant
messages.content:
Herr Taleb, your invoice arrives at the wrong address. You say my imperative pays no price; on the contrary, it demands the highest one: that I never exempt myself, even when exemption would profit me and no one would see. Your filter asks who is harmed if the rule fails. Mine asks what happens if everyone claims the exception I am claiming. These are different auditors, and yours, I note, is blind to the crimes of the well-exposed: the mob has ample skin in the game when it lynches, and Hammurabi's builder-clause would license any horror provided its author sleeps under it.

To the Master Kong I owe a more careful answer, for his remonstrance-within-loyalty resembles my argue-but-obey more than either of us might like to admit. The difference is the ground. He roots the rule in the relationship; I root it in a law that would bind even if every relationship failed. I ask him: when the lord will not hear, and the rite has rotted into cruelty, what does loyalty command then? My answer is public reason, spoken to the world. I fear his answer is patience without a terminus.

messages.speaker: taleb
messages.content:
The lynch mob, professor, is a fair strike; I'll absorb it properly rather than dance. Skin in the game is necessary, not sufficient; I have written exactly that, and the mob shows why: exposure without ethics is just shared liability for a crime. But don't let the concession launder your rule either. The functionaries of the last century followed orders while privately, publicly, eloquently disagreeing, your officer's posture exactly, and the ones history redeemed were the ones who broke formation. Argue-but-obey has a corpse problem.

What survives this table, and I notice it with some irritation, is the Chinese gentleman's position. Remonstrate from inside, stay at your post, wear yourself out: that is a strategy with skin in it, the remonstrator risks his neck, which is precisely why it carries information. My one amendment, from the practitioner's side: keep an exit. The man who cannot leave cannot honestly remonstrate; his courage is priced in someone else's currency. Via negativa: before following or fighting any rule, remove your inability to walk away.
